item.title: World shares log modest losses as investors assess impact on AI sector from the Nvidia scandal
item.description: HONG KONG — Shares were mostly lower Friday in Europe and Asia, but losses remained modest as investors assessed how Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO might affect the global artificial ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: Stocks swung sharply in morning trading Friday as Wall Street remains on track for its first winning week since early October. Major indexes have been unsteady throughout the week as AI-focused companies pushed and pulled the market. Many of those companies have big stock values with a heavier impact on the market’s gains or losses. The S&P 500 shifted from modest moves at the opening of trading to a 1 per cent drop. The index still remains on track for a weekly gain of 1.9 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 67 points, or 0.1 per cent, as of 10:37 a.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite fell 1.8 per cent. The market remains unsteady a day after the AI industry was rocked by the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The company has been the face of the AI industry, which has been responsible for much of the gains, and big swings, on Wall Street. Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised U.S. national security concerns. Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO. The AI industry’s influence over Wall Street was evident again Friday. More stocks within the S&P 500 were rising rather than falling, but a slump for technology stocks with a big focus on AI dragged indexes lower. Nvidia was again among the heaviest weights and it fell 4.1 per cent. Broadcom fell 6.6 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 10 per cent. Nvidia in particular has been slipping for weeks amid wider concerns about a potential slowdown for the industry. The big worry has been whether AI will produce enough profit to justify the costly investments and big stock values. Outside of AI, Microsoft had a more modest 0.1 per cent loss, despite suffering a global outage for its web services that disrupted email accounts and other applications. Oil prices rose a day after U.S. President Donald Trump said that the U.S. didn’t “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on. Brent crude, the international standard, was up 0.8 per cent at US$96.63 a barrel on Friday. It was trading near US$72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began. Stocks in Europe and Asia were mixed. Treasury yields were mixed in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, rose to 5.13 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. The yield on the two-year Treasury fell to 4.84 per cent from 4.86 per cent late Thursday. It closely tracks expectations for action from the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December meeting in an effort to cool stubbornly hot inflation. A report on Friday showed that wholesale inflation cooled a bit last month, but remains very high. ___ Damian J. Troise, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Chan Ho-Him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

item.title: World oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover, IEA says
item.description: The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: LONDON -- The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialized countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. “The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the agency said in the report. Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude was last down 0.1 per cent at US$95.71 a barrel. The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack. The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million bpd of crude in October, OPEC said on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September and 97 per cent of the pre-war February volume. Other analysts see signs of surplus Other analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd in October. High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7 million bpd in 2026 to 102.3 million bpd before rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts. As well as rising output from OPEC+, the IEA flagged supply rising from outside the group. Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana will rise by 1.6 million bpd this year, the IEA said. In 2027, global supply is projected to rise by 6.6 million bpd to 108.1 million bpd, led by a further recovery in Gulf output. Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1 million bpd from last month’s report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a U.S. blockade that has curbed its oil exports. For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8 million bpd, slightly down from a 3.94 million bpd surplus last month. (Reporting by Alex Lawler; Editing by Joe Bavier, Elaine Hardcastle, Kirsten Donovan)

item.title: Canada-U.S. travel turnoff reversing after U.S. midterm elections
item.description: Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — The Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States, counteracting the effect of the recent trade war flare-up, travel experts say. Canadian return trips from America rose three per cent in October compared with the same period last year, the seventh-straight month of growth, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Canada. However, the increase marked a smaller uptick than the levels seen through much of the summer and into September. At Flight Centre Travel Group Canada, new leisure bookings — distinct from trips taken — fell 26 per cent year-over-year last month in response to a fresh round of tariffs and taunts by U.S. President Donald Trump weeks earlier. “It really just shows you how fragile cross-border travel is, specifically from the leisure market,” said Amra Durakovic, a spokesperson for the travel agency. Over the past week though, Flight Centre has seen signs of a return to the Canada-U.S. tourism rebound in the wake of the Democrats’ electoral success on Nov. 3, widely viewed as a rebuke to White House policies. “We are hearing a degree of cautious optimism from some travellers who were reluctant to return,” Durakovic said. “One customer, he booked a Mississippi River cruise, and they did that instead of exploring another European holiday,” she said. “Tuesday’s election, that influenced their decision. They said that they definitely feel a lot more comfortable travelling to the U.S. now.” For now, Canadian visitor volumes remain far below levels from 2024 — 27 per cent below in October — as the trade war drags on and Canadians opt for other destinations. Nonetheless, the torrent of votes for Democratic candidates from Kansas to the Carolinas set off flickers of a possible revival in stateside travel, or perhaps signs of what a Democratic triumph in 2028 could herald for tourism. “Pickup to the U.S. has happened in the last week — people that weren’t going to go,” said Marty Firestone, noting an abrupt rise in business at the insurance firm he heads, Travel Secure Inc. “There was a real bad feeling last year: ‘I’m not going there. That man doesn’t want us. He calls us the 51st state,’” Firestone said, describing the attitude of many Canadians. “With the Democratic blue tsunami, as they call it, I think that Canadians are somewhat feeling a little more relieved about going back to the U.S.” Others say it’s too early to gauge whether the midterms revamped interest in cross-border trips. “We need at least a month,” said Richard Vanderlubbe, who heads Hamilton-based travel agency Tripcentral.ca. Even if an upward shift is underway, he suspects it’s a minor one, with Trump set to remain in the Oval Office for two more years. “I don’t feel like there’s a sea change. It’s not like the phones lit up on Wednesday morning with emails flying and, ‘Hey, OK, it’s good to go to the States now.’” The ill feeling is strong enough that some travel agencies avoid promoting American packages altogether. “We just don’t know which of our customers is going to be wildly offended by any kind of marketing in the United States … so we just don’t do it,” Vanderlubbe said. “To market the U.S. is like dynamite.” Flight volumes from Canada to Florida, Arizona, Nevada and California are down 17 per cent in total this quarter versus the final three months of 2024, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Overall Canada-U.S. flight volumes decreased only 10 per cent, revealing the bigger drop in demand for sun-splashed leisure hot spots. Corporate travel continues to hum along, Durakovic said, with virtually no drop in Flight Centre bookings over the past couple of years. “It’s still business as usual. You can’t exactly stop travelling to the U.S. because of politics,” she said. The broader Canadian aversion to travelling south of the border combined with the shutdown of Cuban resorts amid a fuel shortage caused by an American oil blockade has pushed sun seekers farther afield. Mexico, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica have surged in popularity, travel agents said. Portugal and Spain have also enjoyed a recent boost in Canadian visitors. “Air Transat flights to Malaga are full,” said Sal Lato, who owns the Voyages Marlin travel agency franchise. Meanwhile, the leisure airline has cut the 36 flights a week it operated between Canada and Florida in late 2024 down to zero. Not all winter escapees can simply point their finger at a fresh spot on the map and jet off for a getaway, extended or otherwise. “There are still deep ties to many U.S. snowbird destinations,” said Stephen Fine, founder of Snowbird Advisor Insurance. “They have friends who’ve been going there for years and they want to be able to spend their winters with that community,” he said of many Canadians. “A lot of them own properties there. People want to drive down to their destination or have their vehicles with them for the winter,” he noted. For them, America may be the only option. --- Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.
